headline: Leaked draft shows ambition and limits of UK-EU Brexit reset ahead of Friday's Brussels summit

terms.meaning: A push by the UK and EU to rebuild closer ties after Britain left the EU.
A plan to let young people live and work in each other's territory for a limited time.
A system that puts a price on pollution so firms pay for the carbon they release.

levels.headline: Leaked draft shows ambition and limits of UK-EU Brexit reset ahead of Friday's Brussels summit
levels.body:
Leaders from the United Kingdom and the European Union meet in Brussels on Friday 20 November for a summit that could mark a decisive break with the Brexit era. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office in July after Keir Starmer resigned, has made rebuilding relations with Europe a priority.
A leaked draft shows a clear timeline for a Youth Experience Scheme, which would let young people live in each other's territory for up to three years. The aim is to agree it by 2028 at the latest and have it running by January 2030. Participant numbers are undecided, with sources suggesting around 100,000.
Sticking points remain over a deal to integrate the UK into the EU electricity market, where Brussels wants access tied to a financial contribution to funds for its poorest regions. Both sides commit to concluding talks in 2027. On Monday Mr Burnham said Brexit had not worked and that Britain had lost more than it gained.
levels.why: The outcome could shape trade, energy bills and opportunities for young people for years.

levels.headline: Leaked draft reveals what the UK and EU may agree at Friday's summit
levels.body:
UK and EU leaders meet in Brussels on Friday 20 November for a summit that could mark a clear break from the Brexit era. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, in office since July, has made closer relations with Europe a priority and said on Monday that Brexit has not worked.
A leaked draft sets out a timeline for a Youth Experience Scheme allowing young people to live in each other's territory for up to three years. The aim is to seal the agreement by 2028 and have the scheme running by January 2030. Sources say about 100,000 people might take part, though that is not settled.
The hardest issue is a deal to link the UK to the EU electricity market. Brussels wants Britain to pay towards funding for the bloc's poorest regions in return for access. Both sides promise to finish negotiations in 2027. Mr Burnham plans a national conversation on the long-term relationship afterwards.
levels.why: The outcome could shape trade, energy bills and opportunities for young people for years.

levels.headline: What the UK and EU could agree at the Brussels summit on Friday
levels.body:
The United Kingdom and the European Union hold a summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November that could mark a turning point after Brexit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who became leader in July, wants a much closer relationship with Europe. On Monday he said Brexit had not delivered what was promised.
According to a leaked draft, the two sides would set a timetable for a scheme letting young people live in each other's territory for up to three years. They hope to agree it by 2028, with the scheme starting by January 2030. About 100,000 places are mentioned, but the number is not final.
One big disagreement is over linking Britain to the EU electricity market. The EU wants a payment towards funding for its poorest regions in return. Both sides say they will finish those talks in 2027. Mr Burnham has said he will start a national debate on Britain's long-term ties with Europe after the summit.
levels.why: The outcome could shape trade, energy bills and opportunities for young people for years.

levels.headline: UK and EU leaders prepare for a summit to rebuild ties after Brexit

Leaders from Britain and the European Union meet in Brussels on Friday 20 November. The summit could be a big step away from the years of tension that followed Brexit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took over in July, says rebuilding links with Europe is a priority. On Monday he said that Brexit has not worked and that Britain has lost more than it has gained.
A leaked draft suggests a plan for young people to live in each other's countries for up to three years. The idea is to agree it by 2028 and start it by January 2030. Around 100,000 people might take part, though nobody has settled the number.
The tricky part is electricity. Britain wants to join the EU's shared power market, but Brussels wants a payment towards help for its poorest regions. Both sides say they will finish those talks in 2027.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU meet on Friday to try to get closer after Brexit
levels.body:
Leaders from Britain and the European Union (the group of 27 European countries) meet in Brussels on Friday 20 November. They want to improve relations after Brexit, when Britain left the EU. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who became prime minister in July, says closer ties with Europe are a priority. He has said Brexit has not worked well.
A leaked draft, which is a copy of a plan that was not meant to be public yet, shows one idea. Young people could live in each other's countries for up to three years. This might be agreed by 2028 and begin by January 2030. About 100,000 people could take part.
One problem is electricity. Britain wants to share the EU's power market. The EU wants Britain to pay something towards helping poorer areas of Europe. They plan to finish these talks in 2027.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe meet to talk about being closer again
levels.body:
On Friday 20 November, leaders from Britain and the European Union meet in Brussels. The EU is the group of European countries that Britain left a few years ago, in what people call Brexit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants to rebuild closer links. He says that leaving has not worked well.
A leaked plan, which is a paper that was not meant to be seen yet, shows one idea. Young people could live in each other's countries for up to three years. It might be agreed by 2028 and begin by January 2030. Around 100,000 people could take part.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU will meet to talk about working more closely
levels.body:
On Friday 20 November, leaders from Britain and the European Union will meet in Brussels. The EU is a group of European countries that work together on trade and rules. Britain left the group in an event called Brexit. Now the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, wants a closer friendship with it again. He says Brexit has not worked well for Britain.
A leaked plan, which is a secret paper that has been shared by accident, shows one idea. Young people from Britain and Europe could live in each other's countries for up to three years. That could start by January 2030, and perhaps 100,000 people might take part.

levels.headline: Britain and its European neighbours are trying to be better friends

On Friday, leaders from Britain and the EU will meet in a city called Brussels. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, says leaving has not worked well and he wants to work more closely with Europe.
A secret plan has been shared by accident. It says young people might be able to live in each other's countries for up to three years. This would not start until 2030. About 100,000 young people might be allowed to do it.
There is one big problem. Britain wants to share Europe's electricity. The EU wants Britain to pay for it. They will keep talking until 2027.

levels.headline: Britain wants to be closer friends with Europe again
levels.body:
Some years ago, Britain left a big group of countries in Europe called the European Union. Now the person in charge of Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, wants to be closer friends with them again. He says leaving did not work out well. On Friday he and the EU leaders will meet in a city called Brussels to talk about it.
One idea is that young people could go and live in another country for up to three years. It would not start for a few years, in 2030. Maybe 100,000 young people could do it.
They also talk about sharing electricity, which is the power that lights our homes. The EU wants Britain to pay some money for it. They both say they will finish talking about it in 2027.
levels.why: The outcome could shape trade, energy bills and opportunities for young people for years.

levels.headline: Britain and its neighbours want to be friends again
levels.body:
Imagine two groups of friends who stopped playing together at school. Britain is one group. The other group is a club of countries in Europe. Britain left the club a few years ago. Now Britain's new leader, Andy Burnham, wants them to play together more. On Friday they will meet to talk.
One idea is a big adventure for young people. They could go and live in another country for up to three years. It would begin a few years from now. About 100,000 young people might get to go.
They also need to agree about sharing electricity, which gives us light and warmth. The club wants Britain to give some money to share it, a bit like paying for a shared toy. They will keep talking until 2027.
levels.why: The outcome could shape trade, energy bills and opportunities for young people for years.

headline: S&P 500 falls for fifth straight session as Nvidia slides; Nasdaq edges higher

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 of the biggest companies listed in the United States.
An index of shares on the Nasdaq exchange, heavy with technology companies.
The average closing price over 200 trading days, which investors use to judge a market's trend.

levels.headline: S&P 500 falls for fifth straight session as Nvidia slides; Nasdaq edges higher
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Wednesday 18 November, the latest completed trading session, falling 0.23% to 7,323.63. It was the fifth consecutive daily loss for the broad index and its longest losing run since June.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561.25 points, or 1.11%, to 50,198.17, as shares in Nvidia slid even after the chipmaker beat analysts' profit and revenue forecasts for its third quarter. The Nasdaq Composite bucked the trend, rising 0.42% to 24,429.88.
Energy was the weakest part of the S&P 500, falling almost 3%. The index's close on Tuesday was its first below its 200-day average since 7 April, a level traders watch as a sign of the market's direction. The week has been volatile, with the Dow down more than 800 points on Monday and by 848.75 points on Tuesday. Investors are also weighing fears of higher interest rates.
levels.why: US share prices affect pensions and savings and signal how confident investors are about the economy.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% in October as fuel prices push up the annual rate

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main official measure of how fast prices rise.
Inflation leaving out food and energy, which can swing sharply.
The prices firms pay for materials and fuel, or charge for goods leaving factories.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% in October as fuel prices push up the annual rate
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 3.5% in September, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday. Prices rose 0.5% on the month. Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said fuel prices were again a major contributor.
Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.8%, little changed. Services inflation was 3.7%. CPIH, which includes housing costs, rose to 3.7%, and the RPI measure was 4.2%. Food inflation fell to 0.9%, with food and non-alcoholic drink prices rising at the slowest pace in five years.
Pressure is building further back in the supply chain. Producer input prices, the cost of materials and fuel for businesses, rose 10.8% in the year to October, up from 8.3% in September. The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% on 5 November, warning inflation could near 5% by mid-2027.
levels.why: Rising prices reduce what wages and savings can buy and influence interest rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation edges up to 3.6% as fuel costs climb
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics reported on Wednesday that consumer price inflation reached 3.6% in the year to October 2026, from 3.5% in September. Prices rose 0.5% over the month. The ONS chief economist, Grant Fitzner, said fuel was once more a major reason for the rise.
Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was steady at 2.8%, while services inflation was 3.7%. The CPIH measure, which counts housing costs, was 3.7%, and the older RPI measure was 4.2%. Food inflation eased to 0.9%, the slowest rise in food and non-alcoholic drink prices in five years.
Business costs are rising faster. Producer input prices went up 10.8% in the year to October, compared with 8.3% a month earlier. The Bank of England lifted its main rate to 4% on 5 November and warned inflation could approach 5% by the middle of 2027.
levels.why: Rising prices reduce what wages and savings can buy and influence interest rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as petrol and diesel prices climb
levels.body:
Prices in the United Kingdom were 3.6% higher in October than a year earlier, according to the Office for National Statistics. That is up from 3.5% in September. Over the month alone, prices rose 0.5%. The ONS said fuel prices were once again a major reason.
Core inflation, which leaves out volatile items such as energy and food, stayed at 2.8%. Prices for services, such as restaurants and travel, rose 3.7%. Food was the bright spot: food inflation fell to 0.9%, with food and soft drinks rising at the slowest pace in five years.
Costs for businesses are climbing faster. The price of materials and fuel bought by firms rose 10.8% in the year to October, up from 8.3%. The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% earlier this month and said inflation could get close to 5% by the middle of next year.

levels.headline: UK prices are rising a little faster, mainly because of fuel
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics, which produces official figures, said prices in the UK were 3.6% higher in October than a year before. Inflation, the speed at which prices rise, was 3.5% in September, so it has crept up. The main reason was the rising cost of petrol and diesel.
Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy because they can jump around, stayed at 2.8%. Food prices were rising much more slowly, at only 0.9%, the slowest in five years.
Companies are facing higher bills too. What firms pay for materials and fuel rose 10.8% in the year to October, up from 8.3%. This often leads to higher shop prices later. The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% this month, and it warns that inflation could reach nearly 5% by the middle of 2027.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are going up a bit faster because of petrol and diesel

Inflation means prices going up over time. The Office for National Statistics said prices in the UK were 3.6% higher in October than a year earlier. In September the figure was 3.5%. The main reason was the cost of petrol and diesel, which has risen. That means filling up a car costs more.
Not everything is getting dearer quickly. Food prices rose by just 0.9%, which is the slowest in five years. Another measure, which leaves out food and energy, stayed at 2.8%.
Businesses are paying much more for their materials and fuel, 10.8% more than a year ago. Shops may pass some of this on to customers later. The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4% to try to keep prices under control.

levels.headline: Things in the UK cost a bit more than last year

But food prices only went up a tiny bit. That is good news for families who buy food each week.
Shops and factories also pay more for what they need, and they may charge us more later. A big bank called the Bank of England is trying to help. It made borrowing money cost more. That can slow down price rises, a bit like putting a brake on a bike.

levels.headline: Why some things in the UK cost a bit more now

Petrol and diesel, which cars use, cost more. But food went up only a tiny bit.
The shops and factories also pay more for things they need, so they may charge more later. A big bank called the Bank of England is trying to slow this down. It makes borrowing money cost more, a bit like asking for a bigger thank-you for lending a pencil.

headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% for first time in over three years, warning inflation could near 5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings.
The Monetary Policy Committee, the nine-member group that sets the rate.
One hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is 0.25%.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% for first time in over three years, warning inflation could near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate by 25 basis points to 4% on 5 November, its first increase in more than three years. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1, with the one dissenter wanting a larger rise of 50 basis points to 4.25%.
The Bank tied the decision to the conflict in the Middle East and its effect on energy prices. In its quarterly forecasts it warned inflation could reach around 5% by the middle of 2027, up from 3.5% in September. Governor Andrew Bailey said the increase should not be seen as the first of an inevitable long sequence of rises, but that unless the conflict is resolved, it does not seem likely to be the last.
Higher rates make mortgages and loans more expensive for many households and businesses, while giving savers better returns. The move follows rate rises elsewhere this year, including from the European Central Bank.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts rates to 4% and warns inflation could approach 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on 5 November. It was the first increase in more than three years. Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed the move, and one wanted a bigger rise to 4.25%.
The Bank linked its decision to the Middle East conflict and higher energy prices. New forecasts show inflation could reach about 5% by mid-2027, compared with 3.5% in September. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the start of a long series, but added that unless the conflict ends it does not look like the last.
The change affects borrowers and savers. Mortgage and loan costs are likely to rise for many people, while savings rates may improve. The ECB has also raised its rates this year.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates for the first time in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its key interest rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November, the first rise in more than three years. Of the nine members who set the rate, eight voted for it and one wanted a bigger rise to 4.25%.
The Bank blamed the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up energy costs. It now thinks inflation could reach around 5% by the middle of 2027, up from 3.5% in September. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise was not the first of an inevitable long sequence, but that unless the conflict is resolved it did not seem likely to be the last.
For ordinary people, higher interest rates usually mean dearer mortgages and loans, but better rewards for people with savings. The aim is to cool spending and stop prices rising too fast.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates for the first time in three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate to 4% from 3.75%. This happened on 5 November and it is the first rise in over three years. Eight of the nine people on the committee that sets the rate voted for it. One wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank said the war in the Middle East is pushing up the price of energy, and that this feeds through to prices in shops. It now expects inflation, the rate at which prices rise, to reach nearly 5% by the middle of 2027. In September it was 3.5%. Governor Andrew Bailey said this is not necessarily the first of many rises, but more could follow if the conflict continues.
Higher rates make loans and mortgages dearer. They also help people with savings earn a little more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises its interest rate to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. It sets a main interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. On 5 November it raised that rate to 4% from 3.75%. This is the first time it has gone up in over three years. Eight members of its committee voted yes and one wanted an even bigger rise.
The Bank did this because of the war in the Middle East. The war has made energy more expensive, which pushes prices up. The Bank thinks prices could be rising by nearly 5% a year by the middle of 2027. The Governor, Andrew Bailey, said more rises might come if the war goes on.
Higher rates mean mortgages and loans cost more. People with savings may earn more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% to slow rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. On 5 November it raised its main interest rate, the price of borrowing money, from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first rise in over three years. Eight members of the committee voted for it and one wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank said the war in the Middle East is pushing up energy costs, and that this feeds into shop prices. It thinks inflation, the speed at which prices rise, could reach nearly 5% by the middle of 2027. Governor Andrew Bailey said more rises could follow if the conflict goes on.
Higher rates make mortgages and loans cost more. They can also give savers a little more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a very important bank that looks after the UK's money. It sets an interest rate. This is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. On 5 November, it raised the rate to 4%. It was the first rise for more than three years. Eight people voted yes and one wanted a bigger rise.
The reason is the war in the Middle East. It has made fuel and energy cost more, so prices in shops go up. The Bank thinks prices might rise by almost 5% a year by mid-2027. It wants to slow that down.
When the rate goes up, loans and mortgages cost more. But people who save money may earn a bit more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has made borrowing money cost more
levels.body:
When you borrow money, you usually pay back a bit extra. This extra is called interest. The Bank of England decides how high the main interest rate should be. On 5 November it raised the rate to 4%. It is the first time it has gone up in over three years.
The Bank did this because there is a war in the Middle East. The war makes things like fuel more expensive. That makes lots of things in shops cost more too. The Bank thinks prices could go up by nearly 5% a year by 2027.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less. This can slow price rises. It can be hard for families with loans or mortgages. People who save may get a little more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: The Bank of England asks people to borrow less
levels.body:
Banks lend money and ask for a little extra back, called interest. The Bank of England is the boss bank that decides how high the interest should be. On 5 November it made it a bit higher, 4%. This is the first time it has done that in three years.
It did this because a war far away is making fuel cost more. When fuel costs more, many things in shops cost more too. The Bank wants to stop prices going up too fast.
If borrowing costs more, grown-ups think harder before they borrow, so less money gets spent. That can calm prices down. But families who owe money may find it harder to pay. People who save may earn a bit more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

levels.headline: The boss bank makes borrowing a bit more expensive
levels.body:
Imagine you lend a friend a pencil and ask for a little extra back as a thank-you. The extra is like interest. A big bank called the Bank of England decides how big that thank-you should be for grown-ups who borrow money. This month it made the thank-you bigger.
It did this because a war far away has made fuel cost more. When fuel costs more, many things in shops cost more as well, like a snack in the playground getting dearer. The bank wants prices to stop going up too fast.
If borrowing costs more, grown-ups spend less. That can slow price rises down. But it is harder for families who owe money. People who save may earn a little more.
levels.why: The rate affects mortgage payments, loans and savings returns for millions of people.

headline: Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill passes Commons Third Reading by 290 votes to 94

terms.meaning: The final vote on a bill in the House of Commons before it passes to the Lords.
The UK's second parliamentary chamber, which examines and can amend bills.
The number of votes by which the winning side beats the other.

levels.headline: Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill passes Commons Third Reading by 290 votes to 94
levels.body:
The Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill passed its Third Reading in the House of Commons by 290 votes to 94, a majority of 196, according to the government. The Third Reading is the last Commons vote on a bill, and it now moves to the House of Lords for scrutiny.
The government has described the legislation as landmark immigration reforms. In the Lords, peers can examine the bill line by line, suggest amendments and send it back to the Commons, although the elected chamber has the final say in most cases.
The bill is one of the most closely watched pieces of legislation in this Parliament, given the strong public interest in immigration and asylum policy. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is also preparing for a summit with the European Union in Brussels on Friday, where migration and youth mobility are part of the wider discussion.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: Immigration and Asylum Bill clears the Commons and moves to the Lords
levels.body:
The Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill passed its Commons Third Reading by 290 votes to 94, a majority of 196. Third Reading is the final Commons vote on a bill, and it now goes to the House of Lords.
The government calls the bill landmark immigration reform. In the Lords, peers will examine it in detail, can propose changes and can send it back to MPs, although the Commons usually has the final say.
Immigration and asylum are subjects of strong public interest, so the bill is closely watched. It comes in the same week that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government prepares for a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where youth mobility is among the topics being discussed.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: Home Secretary's immigration reforms pass the Commons and go to the Lords
levels.body:
MPs have passed the Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill at its Third Reading, by 290 votes to 94. The majority of 196 shows strong backing in the House of Commons. Third Reading is the final vote in the Commons, after which the bill goes to the House of Lords.
The government has called the bill landmark reform of the immigration system. In the Lords, members will go through the bill in detail and may suggest changes. Any changes go back to the Commons, which normally has the last word.
Immigration and asylum are among the most debated issues in British politics. The vote comes as the government prepares for a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: MPs vote for new immigration laws, which now go to the House of Lords
levels.body:
MPs in the House of Commons have voted for the Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill. The vote was 290 for and 94 against, so the bill won by 196 votes. A bill is a proposed new law. This was its Third Reading, the final Commons vote.
The government says the bill is a landmark reform of how immigration works. Next, it goes to the House of Lords, a second group of lawmakers who check bills carefully. They can suggest changes, and then MPs decide whether to accept them. Most of the time, MPs have the last word.
Immigration and asylum are topics many people care about. The vote came shortly before a summit between Britain and the EU in Brussels on Friday.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: The Commons votes for a new immigration law, and the Lords will look at it next
levels.body:
A bill is an idea for a new law. This one is called the Immigration and Asylum Bill, and it was put forward by the Home Secretary. MPs, who are elected to represent people in the House of Commons, voted on it. 290 voted for it and 94 voted against, so it won by 196 votes.
The government says it is a big change to how immigration works in the UK. Now the bill goes to a second group called the House of Lords. They read it closely and can suggest changes. Then MPs decide what to do with those changes.
People care a lot about immigration and asylum. Asylum is when someone asks for protection in a new country because it is unsafe at home.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: MPs back new immigration and asylum plans, and the Lords look at them next
levels.body:
MPs in the House of Commons have voted for the Home Secretary's Immigration and Asylum Bill. A bill is a plan for a new law. The vote was 290 for and 94 against, a majority of 196. This was the Third Reading, which is the last Commons vote on a bill.
The government calls it a landmark reform of immigration. Immigration is when people move to live in another country. Asylum is when people ask for protection because it is unsafe at home.
The bill now goes to the House of Lords, a second group of lawmakers. They check it in detail and can suggest changes. MPs normally have the final say, so it is not yet law.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: MPs have voted yes to a new law about immigration
levels.body:
A bill is a plan for a new law. This bill is about immigration, which is when people move to live in another country. It also covers asylum. That is when people ask for safety in a new country because home is too dangerous. The bill was written by the Home Secretary, who is a minister in charge of these things.
MPs, who are chosen by voters, voted on it. 290 said yes and 94 said no. That is a big win. Next, the bill goes to the House of Lords. They check it again and can say what should change.
The government says this will make big changes. Many people care about this topic, so lots of people are watching.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: A new law about people moving to the UK passes a big vote
levels.body:
Sometimes people move to a new country to live, and the government makes rules about it. A group of grown-ups called MPs voted on new rules this week. They voted yes by a large number. 290 said yes and only 94 said no. The rules are called the Immigration and Asylum Bill. Asylum means safety for people who cannot stay in their home country.
Now the bill goes to another group called the House of Lords. They look at it carefully. They can say what they would change. Then MPs decide.
The rules are not a law yet. Lots of people care about this because it is about who can come to live in the UK, so many people are watching.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: Grown-ups vote yes on new rules about moving to the UK
levels.body:
Imagine your school wants to change a rule. First, a group of teachers votes on it. Then another group checks it. This week something like that happened in the UK. A group called MPs voted on a new rule about people who move to Britain from other countries. Most of them said yes. 290 said yes and 94 said no.
Some people move because they want a new life. Some come because it is not safe at home, and they ask for help. The bill has rules for both.
Now another group called the House of Lords will look at the rule carefully. They can suggest changes. It is not a law until everyone has agreed.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

levels.headline: Grown-ups make new rules about who can move to the UK
levels.body:
Think about the rules at your school. Someone decides them, and a group votes if they are fair. In the UK, grown-ups called MPs make the big rules for everyone. This week, they voted on new rules about people who want to come and live in Britain. They voted yes. 290 said yes and 94 said no.
Some people come from far away because they are not safe at home. They ask for help and a safe place to live. The rules say how that should work.
Now another group of grown-ups, called the House of Lords, will check the rules too. They are like teachers double-checking homework before it is marked.
levels.why: The bill would change immigration and asylum rules and now faces scrutiny in the Lords.

headline: US-Iran talks via Qatar stall as Tehran threatens shipping in the Strait of Hormuz

terms.meaning: A narrow waterway between the Gulf and the open sea through which a large share of the world's oil passes.
Using warships to stop ships entering or leaving a country's ports.
Processing uranium to make nuclear fuel, which at high levels can also be used for weapons.

levels.headline: US-Iran talks via Qatar stall as Tehran threatens shipping in the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
Indirect talks between the United States and Iran, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, appear to have reached a stalemate, with Hormuz tensions escalating, CNBC reported on 17 November. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy told shipping firms to avoid a US-backed southern route, and an army spokesperson said the strait would not reopen until the enemy accepts Iran's conditions.
The core dispute is over terms. Iran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted and sanctions on its oil exports removed. Washington wants Iran to cut nuclear enrichment. Earlier this month Qatari officials spoke of an interim deal to build trust, and President Trump said the war could end fairly soon, while warning he could reverse course.
The strait matters to the world economy. ANZ research put crude flows through Hormuz at about 60% of normal, and a third US carrier has arrived in the region. A tanker was struck in the strait.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: Talks to end the US-Iran war stall as threats grow around Hormuz
levels.body:
Indirect US-Iran talks, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, have run into a stalemate while tensions rise around the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy has told shipping companies to avoid a US-backed southern route. An army spokesperson said the strait will stay shut until the enemy accepts Iran's conditions.
The two sides disagree on terms. Iran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted and oil sanctions removed. The US wants Iran to reduce nuclear enrichment. Qatar spoke of an interim agreement earlier in November, and President Trump said the war could end fairly soon but that he could change course.
The strait carries a large share of the world's oil. ANZ estimates flows are about 60% of normal. A third US aircraft carrier has arrived and a tanker has been struck.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: US-Iran peace talks stall while tensions rise in the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
Talks between the United States and Iran, passed through Qatar and Pakistan, appear to be stuck. Meanwhile tensions around the Strait of Hormuz are rising. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy has told shipping firms to avoid a route backed by the US. An army spokesperson said the strait would not reopen until the enemy accepts Iran's conditions.
The sides are far apart. Iran wants the US blockade of its ports lifted and sanctions on its oil sales removed. The US wants Iran to reduce its work on nuclear fuel. Earlier this month Qatar said an interim deal was being sought, and President Trump said the war could end fairly soon.
The strait is a major route for oil, and flows are about 60% of normal, according to ANZ. A tanker has been struck and a third US carrier has arrived.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: Efforts to end the US-Iran war are stuck, and shipping is under threat
levels.body:
Talks between the United States and Iran are passing through go-betweens in Qatar and Pakistan. They appear to be stuck. At the same time the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route for oil, is getting more dangerous. Iran's navy has told shipping companies to avoid a route backed by the US. Its army says the strait will stay closed until its conditions are met.
Each side wants something different. Iran wants the US to end its blockade of Iranian ports and drop oil sanctions. The US wants Iran to cut back its nuclear fuel work. President Trump has said the war could end soon, but he has also warned he could change course.
About 60% of the usual oil is moving through the strait. A tanker has been struck.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: Peace talks between the US and Iran are stuck
levels.body:
The US and Iran are in a war, and people from Qatar and Pakistan are trying to help them make peace by carrying messages between them. But the talks seem to be stuck. At the same time, things are getting tense around the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow stretch of sea where lots of the world's oil ships pass.
Iran wants the US to stop blocking its ports and to end the rules stopping it from selling oil. The US wants Iran to cut back on its work to make nuclear fuel. Neither has agreed.
Only about 60% of the normal amount of oil is getting through the strait. A tanker has been hit. This can make fuel cost more in many countries.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: The US and Iran cannot agree on peace, and ships are at risk
levels.body:
The United States and Iran are at war. Qatar and Pakistan are helping by passing messages between the two sides, but the talks seem stuck. Meanwhile, things are getting tense around the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that carries a large share of the world's oil.
Iran wants the US to lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to end sanctions on its oil. A blockade is when warships stop ships going in or out. The US wants Iran to cut its nuclear enrichment, which is the work that makes nuclear fuel. Neither side has given way.
Only about 60% of the normal oil is passing through the strait, and a tanker has been struck. That can push up fuel prices around the world.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: Talks to end the war between the US and Iran are stuck
levels.body:
Two countries, the United States and Iran, are in a war. Helpers from Qatar and Pakistan are trying to bring peace. They pass messages between the two sides. But the talks seem to be stuck. There is also trouble at sea. A narrow water route called the Strait of Hormuz is very important. A lot of the world's oil travels through it in ships.
Iran wants the US to stop blocking its ports and to let it sell oil again. The US wants Iran to make less nuclear fuel. They have not agreed.
Only about 60% of the usual oil is passing through. A tanker has been hit. If less oil gets through, fuel can cost more everywhere.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: The US and Iran cannot agree on how to stop their war
levels.body:
The United States and Iran are fighting a war. Some other countries, like Qatar, are trying to help them stop. They carry messages between the two sides. But the two sides do not agree yet. This matters because of a narrow sea road called the Strait of Hormuz. Many ships carrying oil go through it.
Iran wants the US to stop blocking its ports and let it sell oil. The US wants Iran to make less of something called nuclear fuel, which can be used in bombs. Both say no for now.
A ship carrying oil has been hit. Less oil is getting through. That can make petrol cost more for families all around the world.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: Two countries cannot agree on how to stop fighting
levels.body:
Two countries, the United States and Iran, are in a war. They are like two children arguing in the playground who will not say sorry. Helpers from another country, Qatar, are trying to make peace. They carry messages from one side to the other. But so far it has not worked.
Iran says the US must stop blocking its ports. The US says Iran must stop making a kind of fuel that could be used for bombs.
There is a narrow sea road nearby where lots of oil ships go. Fewer ships can get through now. If less oil gets through, petrol can cost more for families in many places.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

levels.headline: Two countries are still arguing and cannot make peace
levels.body:
Imagine two children who had a big fight in the playground. A teacher from another class is trying to help them make up. She passes messages from one to the other. But they will not agree yet, and they both want something different.
The two countries are the United States and Iran. One wants the other to stop blocking its ports. The other wants it to stop making a kind of fuel that can be used for bombs.
Near where they are fighting there is a narrow sea road. Many ships carrying oil use it, and some of them are not safe. When fewer oil ships get through, petrol can cost more for families like yours.
levels.why: A disrupted Hormuz affects world oil supply, fuel prices and the risk of a wider war.

headline: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge for a second night as peace talks stall over Donbas

terms.meaning: A region of eastern Ukraine, partly held by Russia, at the centre of the territorial dispute.
An agreement to stop fighting.
The bridge linking Russia to the Crimean peninsula, which Russia annexed in 2014.

levels.headline: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge for a second night as peace talks stall over Donbas
levels.body:
Ukrainian drones struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to annexed Crimea for a second consecutive night, forcing its closure, Euronews reported. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the operation unprecedented and said it had been prepared over several weeks.
Peace efforts remain stalled. Talks resumed in Abu Dhabi, but Euronews said a ceasefire was nowhere near. Moscow still demands control of the whole of the Donbas, including areas it has failed to capture, while Kyiv refuses to give up territory. Mr Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas in return for NATO membership.
In Europe, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed a 45 billion euro loan to Ukraine backed by joint debt, while Germany and Norway agreed to buy more US air defences for Ukraine. Russian drones continued to hit Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv and Odesa.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine hits the Kerch Bridge again while talks on ending the war stall
levels.body:
Ukrainian drones hit the Kerch Bridge, which links Russia to annexed Crimea, for a second night running and forced it to close. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it an unprecedented operation that had taken several weeks to prepare.
The diplomacy is stuck. Talks resumed in Abu Dhabi, but Euronews reported a ceasefire is nowhere near. Russia demands the whole of the Donbas, including land it has not captured, and Ukraine refuses to hand over territory. Mr Zelenskyy said the US raised the idea of Ukraine giving up Donbas in exchange for NATO membership.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed a 45 billion euro loan for Ukraine backed by joint EU debt. Germany and Norway agreed to buy more US air defences for Ukraine, and Russian strikes continued on cities including Kyiv and Odesa.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine strikes the Kerch Bridge again as peace talks make little progress
levels.body:
Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with the annexed region of Crimea, with drones for a second night in a row. The bridge was closed. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was an unprecedented operation that took weeks to plan.
Peace talks have started again in Abu Dhabi, but a ceasefire is not close. Russia wants control of the whole Donbas region, even parts it has not taken, and Ukraine will not give up land. Mr Zelenskyy said the US suggested Ukraine give up Donbas in return for a place in NATO.
In Europe, Ursula von der Leyen, who leads the European Commission, proposed a 45 billion euro loan to Ukraine paid for by joint EU borrowing. Germany and Norway will buy more US air defences. Russian drones also hit homes in Kyiv and Odesa.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine hits a key bridge to Crimea again, and peace talks are still stuck
levels.body:
Ukraine used drones to attack the Kerch Bridge for a second night in a row. The bridge joins Russia to Crimea, a region Russia took from Ukraine. It had to close. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack had been planned for weeks and had never been done before.
Peace talks have begun again in Abu Dhabi, but there is no sign of a ceasefire, an agreement to stop fighting. Russia wants all of a region called Donbas. Ukraine says no. Mr Zelenskyy said the US suggested Ukraine give up Donbas in return for joining NATO, a military alliance.
The EU's Ursula von der Leyen has suggested a 45 billion euro loan for Ukraine. Russia kept hitting Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv and Odesa.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine attacks an important bridge, and talks to end the war are stuck
levels.body:
Ukraine used drones to hit a big bridge two nights in a row. The bridge joins Russia to a place called Crimea, which Russia took from Ukraine. The bridge had to close. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it had been planned for weeks.
People are talking in a city called Abu Dhabi to try to end the war. But they are not close to agreeing. Russia wants a whole region of Ukraine called Donbas. Ukraine says it will not give up its land.
Europe is trying to help. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, wants to lend Ukraine 45 billion euros. Russia keeps sending drones at Ukrainian cities, such as Kyiv and Odesa.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine hits a big bridge again, and the war talks are stuck
levels.body:
Ukraine hit a big bridge with drones two nights in a row. The bridge joins Russia to Crimea, a place Russia took from Ukraine years ago. Now it is closed. Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said this had never happened before.
Some people are meeting in a city called Abu Dhabi to talk about stopping the war. They are not close to agreeing. Russia wants a big part of Ukraine called Donbas. Ukraine says no.
Europe wants to help Ukraine. A leader called Ursula von der Leyen wants to lend Ukraine 45 billion euros. But Russia is still sending drones to Ukrainian cities like Kyiv and Odesa, which hurts people who live there.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine hits a bridge, and the war goes on
levels.body:
A war is going on between Russia and Ukraine. Ukraine sent drones, which are small flying machines, to hit a big bridge. The bridge joins Russia to a place called Crimea. It was hit two nights in a row, and now it is closed.
Leaders are meeting in a city called Abu Dhabi to talk about stopping the war. But they do not agree. Russia wants a big part of Ukraine called Donbas. Ukraine says that is its land.
Other countries in Europe want to help Ukraine. They talk about lending it a lot of money. Meanwhile, Russia is still sending drones to cities in Ukraine, which is scary for the families there.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia are still fighting and cannot agree
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine are two neighbouring countries that have been fighting for a long time. This week Ukraine hit a bridge that Russia uses. The bridge is closed now. The leaders of the countries want different things, so they cannot agree to stop.
Russia wants a big piece of Ukraine called Donbas. Ukraine says it is Ukraine's own land and will not give it away. Some leaders have been meeting in a faraway city to talk. They have not fixed it yet.
Other countries in Europe are trying to help Ukraine with money and defences. But Russia is still sending drones to Ukrainian cities, and families are afraid.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Two neighbours are fighting and cannot agree to stop
levels.body:
Think of two neighbours who are arguing over a piece of garden. Russia and Ukraine are two neighbouring countries, and they have been fighting for a long time. This week one of them hit a bridge that the other uses. Now the bridge is closed.
Russia says it wants a big piece of Ukraine called Donbas. Ukraine says that piece is its own and will not give it away. Some grown-ups from other places are meeting to help them make up. They have not agreed yet.
Other countries want to lend Ukraine money to help it. But the fighting still goes on, and that is frightening for children who live there.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

levels.headline: Two neighbours are arguing over a piece of garden
levels.body:
Imagine two neighbours who share a fence. They have been arguing for a very long time. One says that a piece of the garden belongs to him. The other says it does not. They are Russia and Ukraine, and they are countries, not people.
This week one neighbour broke a bridge that the other likes to use. Now nobody can use it. Some friendly grown-ups are meeting to help them make up. But they cannot agree yet.
Other friends want to give Ukraine some money to help. But the arguing is still going on. That is sad and frightening for the children who live there. We hope they will say sorry and be friends soon.
levels.why: The war's course and Europe's support shape security and costs across the continent.

headline: Oil steady near $92 a barrel as supply surplus offsets Gulf war risks

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for a barrel of oil.
When more oil is being produced than the world needs.
The International Energy Agency, which advises countries on energy.

levels.headline: Oil steady near $92 a barrel as supply surplus offsets Gulf war risks
levels.body:
Brent crude futures traded around $92.12 a barrel early on Thursday 19 November, up 17 cents or 0.18%, according to CNBC. On Wednesday Brent fell to $91.68, down 1.57%, according to Trading Economics.
Prices have fallen sharply this month. Brent is down about 16% over the past month and settled at $104.77 on 2 November after losing 7.6% that day on hopes of Iran peace talks. The fall reflects expectations of a supply glut. The International Energy Agency expects global supply to exceed demand by more than 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover.
The downside is limited by continuing Iran-related shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices matter for petrol and diesel costs, and fuel was the main driver of UK inflation rising to 3.6% in October. Brent remains well above last year's level.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating costs and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices hold near $92 as a supply glut weighs against Gulf risks
levels.body:
Brent crude traded at around $92.12 a barrel early on Thursday 19 November, up 17 cents, or 0.18%. A day earlier it had fallen 1.57% to $91.68.
Oil has dropped sharply this month. Brent is down about 16% over the past month and on 2 November it settled at $104.77 after losing 7.6% on hopes for Iran peace talks. Traders expect a surplus of oil. The International Energy Agency forecasts supply exceeding demand by more than 1.7 million barrels a day in the final quarter as Middle East exports recover.
Attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz limit how far prices can fall. Oil feeds through to petrol and diesel prices, which pushed UK inflation up in October. Prices remain well above last year's level.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating costs and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices steady around $92 a barrel as a supply surplus weighs on the market
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main international oil price, traded at about $92.12 a barrel on Thursday 19 November, up 0.18%. On Wednesday it fell 1.57% to $91.68.
Prices have dropped a lot this month. Brent is down roughly 16% in a month and was above $104 on 2 November. The fall is because experts expect a surplus of oil. The International Energy Agency says supply could exceed demand by more than 1.7 million barrels a day in the last three months of the year as exports from the Middle East recover.
The fall is held back by attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices affect petrol, diesel and heating costs, so changes feed through to inflation. Fuel pushed UK inflation up in October.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating costs and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices stay near $92 a barrel as there is more oil than the world needs
levels.body:
Brent crude, the oil price used around the world, is about $92 a barrel, and it moved very little on Thursday 19 November. On Wednesday it dropped 1.57%.
Prices have fallen a lot this month, by around 16%. On 2 November they were above $104. The reason is that experts think there will be more oil than the world needs. headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for the first time in three years as another ECB rate rise looms

terms.meaning: The group of EU countries that share the euro as their currency.

levels.headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for the first time in three years as another ECB rate rise looms
levels.body:
Inflation across the euro zone rose to 4% in October, up from 3.8% in September, according to Eurostat's flash estimate. It is the first time it has reached that level in three years.
Energy is the main driver. Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier, and the conflict in the Middle East is cited as the cause of the shock. Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was steady at 2.5%.
The European Central Bank has raised rates twice this year, in June and September, taking its deposit rate to 2.5%. It held on 29 October, with President Christine Lagarde saying policymakers discussed another rise but agreed unanimously to wait. Markets widely expect a quarter-point increase at the 16 to 17 December meeting. Ms Lagarde has also announced she will step down in February. The next flash estimate is due on 1 December.
levels.why: Higher euro zone inflation points to more ECB rate rises and affects UK trade partners.

headline: UK average house prices rise 1.2% to £273,000 in year to September, with London down 3.5%

terms.meaning: An early figure that may be revised when more data arrives.

levels.headline: UK average house prices rise 1.2% to £273,000 in year to September, with London down 3.5%
levels.body:
Average UK house prices rose by 1.2% to £273,000 in the 12 months to September 2026, according to provisional estimates from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The annual rate was unchanged from the 12 months to August.
London was the weakest region, with prices there falling 3.5% over the year. The ONS publishes the figures in its Private rent and house prices bulletin, using information from sales and mortgage records.
Prices are growing slowly. Annual house price growth of 1.2% is well below the 3.6% rate of consumer price inflation in October, so in real terms homes are getting cheaper. The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% on 5 November, which usually makes mortgages dearer and can weigh on demand for homes. The figure for September is provisional and may be revised as more sales data arrives.
levels.why: House prices affect household wealth, and borrowing costs shape who can afford to buy.
